title: Only by deeds
hook: plants and animals differ by kind; humans differ only by what they do

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Salla Sutta, and your line, draw out the dart. Did a memory sting, and did you let it be there? Today two young men walk in mid-argument. Day six hundred four.

Two students, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, have been arguing on a walk. You may remember the name Vasettha from the Long Discourses. One says a person is a brahmin, a member of the priestly class, by birth: pure lineage on both sides, seven generations back. The other says no, it's by conduct. Neither can convince the other. So they do what friends still do when the argument stalls: they go and ask someone they both respect. The Buddha's answer, the ninth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, starts not with people at all but with grass. Today: only by deeds.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `BY BIRTH OR BY CONDUCT?` → `ASK SOMEONE BOTH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Look at grasses and trees, the Buddha says. They don't claim anything, yet their kinds are marked by birth; you can tell one from another. Look at worms, moths, ants. Four-footed animals, small and large. Snakes, fish, birds. Each kind has its own marks, given at birth. Then he turns to humans. Among people, he says, there are no such marks of birth: not in the hair, the head, the ears, the eyes, the mouth, the nose, the lips, the neck, the hands, the feet. Bodies differ, of course; he isn't denying that. But nothing in the body marks out a separate kind. The differences we draw between people are names we give. So what makes someone a farmer? Farming. A trader? Trading. A thief? Stealing. A priest? Performing the rites. And a true brahmin, in the noble sense the Buddha gives the word, is one who has let go, harms no one, is patient, honest, free. Then a line that sounds very modern: the world goes on by action. Beings are bound to their deeds, the poem says, as a moving chariot is held by its linchpin. You've heard a cousin of this before, in the outcast discourse a few weeks back: not by birth, by deeds. Today's version adds the argument from nature. Grass is sorted by kind. People are sorted by what they do. In a society built on birth, that was a bold thing to say out loud.
screen: `GRASS AND BIRDS: MARKED BY BIRTH.` · `PEOPLE: NO SUCH MARKS.` · `A FARMER IS ONE WHO FARMS.` · `THE WORLD GOES ON BY ACTION.` · then, large: `ONLY BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at difference kindly. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone you tend to file under a category: their accent, their job, their family, where they're from. Now set the label down for a moment and ask only, what does this person do? Maybe they're patient with a child. Maybe they show up early. Find one deed. Let the label go quiet and let the deed stand there instead. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Only by deeds. In the Vasettha Sutta, people aren't sorted by birth the way plants and animals are; they're known by what they do. Today's word.
Your line: only by deeds. Today, catch yourself once sizing someone up by where they come from, and look instead for one thing they actually did. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Vasettha Sutta when teaching that worth comes from conduct rather than birth, and in modern India it was important to B. R. Ambedkar and the Buddhist movement he led.

fork.setup: two students ask whether a person is noble by birth or by conduct. where does the Buddha begin his answer?
options: with the family trees of famous priests.
with grasses, trees, insects and animals.
fork.reveal: he starts with nature: plants and animals have marks of kind from birth. people don't, so among people, deeds are what tell.

original.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma): action, deed. in Sn 3.9 the world goes on by kamma.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha just said everyone's equal.
what it means: plants and animals are sorted by kind at birth; people are known by what they do, and the noble one by conduct.
what a scholar hears: the Vasettha Sutta appears both as Sn 3.9 and as MN 98, and redefines 'brahmin' in ethical terms, a move found throughout the early texts.

notes: Sn 3.9 paraphrased. Confirm the list of plants, insects and animals and of body parts, and the linchpin simile (kammanibandhana satta rathass' aniva yayato).
